newsitem.title: USA: Florida says grocers make huge profits on vegetables.
newsitem.headline: Florida says grocers make huge profits on vegetables.

text.p: It may seem incredible to consumers weary of paying more than $1.00 per pound for green beans, but the Florida farmers who grow winter vegetables say their profits on produce are so low that it is barely worth their while.

Survey results released Thursday by the state Department of Agriculture illustrated the reason for the sharp gap between consumers' and producers' views of the winter vegetable market: price markups of as much as 520 percent.

"Fresh produce is being priced out of the reach of many of our citizens," Agriculture Commissioner Bob Crawford said. "And virtually any health study you see recommends that we eat more of it, not less."

Crawford's agency compiled data on both the farm and retail price of eight winter vegetables grown in Florida -- snap beans, cucumbers, sweet corn, eggplant, yellow squash, bell peppers, tomatoes and zucchini -- since this year's growing season began in mid-October.
And it found not only that the markups were high, but that it appeared to be escalating, based on data from farmers and from retailers in the state's five largest metropolitan areas.
For example, during the week of December 9, the farm price of snap beans was $0.35 per pound, and the retail price was $1.04, for an increase of $0.69, or 197.1 percent.
For zucchini, the farm price was $0.16 and the retail price was $0.99, for a markup of $0.83, or 518.7 percent.
Both figures are higher than the average for the season so far, a 188.1 percent markup for snap beans and a 245.7 percent markup for zucchini, according to the department's data.

Crawford called on brokers, shippers and retailers to hold down their costs as much as possible. He also said he would begin next month to provide newspapers and broadcast outlets in Florida with the results of each week's price surveys.
